scenario: AITA For refusing to sit next to a kid with autism during a lecture, and sitting on the floor instead? | I know this sounds bad but bare with me, I’m (23m) in a class that has exactly 30 seats, and there are 31 students. I was running late and walked in a minute before the lecture began. There was only one open seat. I walked over to it and in the next seat over sitting was a kid with autism, he is very socially inept but totally brilliant. The problem is that he smelled like he hadn’t showered in a few weeks, his hair was greasier than Snapes, and he was wearing stained pajamas. I sat next to him for 2 minutes before I was about to gag and I got up and sat on the floor in the back of the lecture hall. The professor saw this and asked if I moved because of the smell, he asked in front of the whole class, I said I just didn’t want to sit there and he continued lecturing. After class a few of the kids said I was TA because I should have just sucked it up for the hour and dealt with the smell. So Reddit AITA?

Your focus on their appearance (rather than their personhood) was dismissive. - **Reinforcing Stigma:** By leaving the seat empty and making the professor address the issue publicly, you contributed to a moment that could have been used to educate the class about neurodiversity instead of shaming the student. - **No Accountability:** You didn’t take responsibility for your role in the situation. This shows growth and accountability. - If you don’t know the student, you could still reflect on how to be more inclusive in the future. 2. **Advocate for Change:** - Talk to the professor (privately) about the need for more accessible seating in the classroom. Frame it as a systemic issue, not a personal one. - If you’re comfortable, share resources about autism and sensory sensitivities with the class (e.g., a short article or video) to foster understanding. 3. **Learn More:** - Educate yourself on autism, neurodiversity, and ableism. But do so in a way that doesn’t disadvantage others. For example, arrive early to secure your preferred spot rather than reacting in the moment. --- ### **Final Thought:** This situation highlights how neurotypical norms often prioritize comfort over inclusion. While it’s okay to have personal boundaries, those boundaries shouldn’t come at the expense of others’ dignity or access to education.
